subject: Archaeology
title: SCUBA and the Birth of Underwater Archaeology
description: A short lesson to help you apply SCUBA and the Birth of Underwater Archaeology.

hook.text: Before SCUBA, underwater archaeology did not exist. Jacques Cousteau's invention in 1943 created an entire field.

buildup.text: Cousteau and Émile Gagnan developed the Aqua-Lung, which let divers breathe freely and work underwater for the first time.

discovery.text: Cousteau led one of the first underwater excavations at Grand Congloué in 1952, recovering Roman amphorae from a wreck.

twist.text: Early divers used airlifts that sucked up artifacts and sediment — destroying context.

climax.text: George Bass pioneered scientific underwater excavation in the 1960s.

punchline.text: Cousteau let us breathe underwater. Bass taught us to think underwater.

quiz.question: Who is considered the pioneer of scientific underwater excavation?
options: Jacques Cousteau, who invented the Aqua-Lung
George Bass, who applied land archaeology methods to underwater sites
Robert Ballard, who discovered the Titanic

details.summary: The invention of SCUBA by Jacques Cousteau and Émile Gagnan in 1943 transformed underwater archaeology from helmet-diving salvage into a rigorous scientific discipline. For the first time, archaeologists could work freely underwater, applying the same careful excavation methods used on land.
details.whyItMatters: SCUBA democratized the underwater world. Before it, only professional divers in heavy equipment could reach wrecks. After Cousteau, trained archaeologists could excavate with precision, turning underwater sites from treasure troves into scientific.
takeaways: SCUBA was co-invented by Cousteau and Gagnan in 1943
It enabled archaeologists to work freely underwater for the first time
Underwater archaeology became a rigorous science rather than salvage

faq.question: Who is considered the founder of underwater archaeology?
faq.answer: George Bass, who conducted the first complete scientific excavation of a shipwreck at Cape Gelidonya, Turkey, in 1960. He proved that underwater sites could be excavated with the same rigor as land sites, establishing standards that define the discipline today.

faq.question: How did SCUBA change archaeology?
faq.answer: Before SCUBA, underwater work required surface-supplied air and heavy helmets that limited mobility. SCUBA freed divers to move naturally, draw site plans, photograph in detail, and excavate carefully. This made true archaeological recording possible on the seafloor for the first time.
